“Aane Do Dilli, Seedha Goli Maar Denge”- Middle-Class Hostility Towards Farmers on the Rise, Turning Violent

As the 2024 Farmers' Protests bring agricultural workers to the borders of Delhi demanding a legally guaranteed MSP, a first report on rising civilian hostility, and on why middle-class apathy towards the protest has become as significant a story as the state's use of teargas and internet shutdowns to suppress it.

By Mouli Sharma

Amid media coverage of the 2024 Farmer’s Protests lending little sympathy to agricultural workers from Delhi bordering states marching to the national capital, & plenty to the government using militant & violent means to suppress them, civilian apathy is profound. This is part one of a report on the public perception of the protest, & speculation over why it is what it is.

POLITICS

UP Higher Judicial Service Rules Amendment: Explanation & Analysis

An explainer on the PIL challenging Uttar Pradesh's 2023 amendment to its Higher Judicial Service Rules, what the amendment changes, why it matters beyond the legal profession, and what courts' increasing convenience with their own regulation signals for accountability under law.

By Mouli Sharma

What does a precedent for such judicial amendments mean for the common man?

A PIL challenging the validity of Rule 5 of UP’s Higher Judicial Service Rules, 1975, in the Allahabad High Court, has brought under scrutiny its 2023 amendment & courts’ increasingly convenient interference with judicial regulation, whose notification was just issued this January. The following article explains why amendments like these affect more than just lawyers & judges, what the common man has at stake, & why speculation over why & how these decisions are taken is necessary to keep lawmaking powers accountable & in check.

UP’s Higher Judicial Service Rules, 1975

Constitutionally, this power (to dictate & amend these rules) is granted to State Governors by Article 309 & Article 233, the latter of which specifically discusses the appointment of district judges, providing that these rules be made in consultation with the respective High Courts of the States. These articles, in accordance with which the rules are written, are a brief & recommended read, attached at the end of the article.

The 2023 Amendment

What was changed?

From LiveLaw.in’s summary of Rule 5 of U.P. Higher Judicial Service Rules, 1975 as amended in the year 2023 with the issuance of the notification dated 11th January 2024:

Rule 5 of the U.P. Higher Judicial Service Rules, 1975 provides for sources of recruitments in High Judiciary. Prior to amendment sub-rule (c) of Rule 5 provided that for direct recruitment from amongst advocates, it was necessary to have a standing of not less than 7 years as on the last date fixed for submission of the application form. By amendment notification dated 11th January 2024, sub-rule (c) was amended to the extent that the words “practicing as an Advocate” replaced the word “standing.” Upasana Agarwal, 2023— Upasana Agarwal, 2023

This refers to the following change:

Rule 5, Sub-rule C, Pre-amendment: “ By direct recruitment from amongst the Advocates of not less than seven years standing on the first day of January next following the year in which the notice inviting applications is published. ”

Continued on page 2 →

“Aane Do Dilli, Seedha Goli Maar Denge”- Middle-Class · continued from page 1

16th February 2024, New Delhi: The 2024 Farmer's Protests come as an outcry against the central government's ignorance & apathy of the nation’s agricultural workers’ issues, with their prime concern being the continued refusal to ensure an MSP to Indian Farmers as was guaranteed in both their 2014 & 2019 manifestos. In anticipation of unrest similar to the last iteration of these protests back in 2021 (wherein as well farmers from Delhi bordering States marched to the national capital in response to three then-recent legislations), the government has taken to an aggressive obstruction of Delhi borders.

But with blockades & armed personnel keeping protesting farmers out of their capital, & internet shutdowns targeting protest centres, the steps taken by the BJP-led government have quickly become less about crowd control & more about shutting down the display completely. Measures that were implemented in the hopes of preventing a violent escalation of conflict like last time have immediately turned violent themselves (read: police fire water cannons at farmers, used aerial drones to deploy teargas).

When the talks on Thursday, like the previous two rounds (on 8th & 12th February), remained inconclusive, farmers again abandoned what was a truce they’d temporarily agreed to for the discussion & stormed the Shambhu border, leading to the infamous clash at the Haryana-Punjab border, where police & paramilitary forces fired tear gas shells & rubber bullets at the crowd for the third time. This was not a regrettable result of sudden & increased agitation, but a planned & repetitive intimidation strategy, as social media accounts of the march’s organisers were suspended beforehand, as were internet services in Haryana & Punjab. The government also shows no signs of regret as till now no public apology has been made, and no justifications given. Rather, to add insult to injury, an order for another 30,000 tear gas shells was placed by the Delhi Police on the same day.

In circumstances like these, where the government itself is doing very little to save face, with the bare minimum of even PR strategies (to be discussed in part two) one would expect public outrage more than or at least close to that during the 2021 protest (which was already not extreme, & this time’s response is far more intensive). Instead, what is being observed across the nation, particularly among the residents of the capital, is widespread hostility. What started with a surprising amount of apathy has soon turned into an even more surprising amount of disgust, resentment, & vitriol against farmers. Interviews conducted by the TVE team within bustling markets & residential areas of the city reveal a disturbing reality: the ‘lying government’ is no longer the common man’s enemy, but anyone who opposes it; even if it’s another common man like himself.

Continued on page 3 →

UP Higher Judicial Service Rules Amendment: Explanatio · continued from page 1

Rule 5, Sub-rule C, Post-amendment: “ By direct recruitment from amongst the Advocates who have been, for not less than seven years, practicing as an Advocate, as on the last date fixed for the submission of application forms;

Provided that only such advocates shall be permitted to appear in the examination process who have been engaged independently for conducting not less than 30 cases (other than bunch cases) for Unreserved categories and 24 cases (other than bunch cases) for Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and Other Backward Classes in the preceding three years, from the year of publication of advertisement for recruitment, before any Court. The certificate of such independent engagement may be issued by District & Sessions Judge of the District or Registrar General/Registrar of High Courts or Secretary General of Supreme Court, as the case may be .” (sic)

Read Upasana Agarwal’s full report of the case here.

What does this mean in layman's terms?

Essentially, the rules now dictate that for the direct recruitment of district & sessions judges, it is necessary for them to have been in practice for no less than 7 years, while merely having the standing of advocate for the same duration would have sufficed before.

This focus on quantifiable experience is further emphasised by the addition of a proviso that, in addition to this 7 years of continuous practice, also requires applicants to have been certifiably engaged in 30 independent cases (24 for reserved categories).

The change that this will bring about is to pull more active lawyers into the courts as judges, & disqualify those who have merely been making the cut due to holding the title of ‘advocate’ as opposed to actively participating.

Is the 2023 Amendment good or bad?

‘It changes things,because obviously, you would prefer a Judge who has been practising for 7 years, rather than someone who's just waited 7 years after acquiring the title & doesn't have any real experience.’ Jia Ahuja, a journalist specialising in information property law, told TVE.

So what is the problem? How does this simple, reasonable amendment, ‘violate the Constitution’?

Why is there a PIL against this change?

Another argument put forth by Pandey’s counsel was with of Sub-rule C (refer to earlier section), calling it ‘arbitrary’ & in violation of article 14 of the Indian Constitution (‘ The State shall not deny to any person equality before the law or the equal protection of the laws within the territory of India .’) Both of these arguments were disputed in the honourable court’s proceedings on the 7th of February, where the defending counsel brought forth an obvious conflict of interest of the petitioner, with Pandey himself being an aspirant of the higher judicial services. Against the claims of constitutional violations, it argued that constitutional articles should not be looked at in ‘isolation’ & that the Indian Constitution holistically supports & encourages the High Court's authority in making legal recommendations.

EDUCATION

Classes on Hold for ‘Viksit Bharat’; Principal Busy in Photo-Op with Modi Cut-Out

At Kalindi College, New Delhi, students were told attendance would be marked for participation in the BJP government's 'Viksit Bharat' initiative, events scheduled during class hours, as the college principal posed for photographs at a Modi cut-out. A ground report on the line between government scheme and institutional compulsion.

By Mouli Sharma

‘Attendance’ to be marked for participation in ‘Viksit Bharat’ events taking place during class hours.

14th February 2024, New Delhi: The current phase of the government’s ‘Viksit Bharat’ ( Developed India ) initiative, “ a nationwide campaign to raise awareness through outreach activities to achieve saturation of schemes of Govt. of India across the country covering all [Local Bodies] ,” is taking place in educational institutes, including higher education institutes like the University of Delhi.

From hours-long photo ops, workshops, surveys & quizzes (take the Viksit Bharat quiz on the Hamara Sankalp Viksit Bharat website to get a certificate from PM Modi himself!) all culminating in the Viksit Bharat Pledge, a wide range of ‘events’ under the sun are taking place in various colleges of Delhi University under the aegis of internal quality assessment committees, media societies, or department management. Some colleges show no participation at all, implying that none of these are regulation procedures, & are being informally implemented. At one Kalindi College, the campaign has taken over day-hours with many of the activities directly clashing with & being given priority over lectures, & overworked faculty canceling several of the rest. But here’s the catch; attendance is still being marked.

With DU’s allotment of 5% of student’s final grade ending up at null for attendance below 67%, & arbitrary cancellation of classes around the year by professors being a regular & consequence-less matter, attending or not attending a 3-hour event can mean the difference between having ‘attended’ or not ‘attended’ 3 lectures at a time on paper, none of which were in fact conducted. This is unfair to students who travel long distances daily Kalindi, one of DU’s many sans-hostel colleges, leading to a large number of students ignoring the ‘mandatory’ attendance of these workshops to stay home & study.

“I haven’t been attending the events. I’m not interested. How many Youth India schemes have come before this? Have they ever improved anything?” says a student of Kalindi College’s Journalism Department, which is the most significantly impacted. One of the more recent departments to suffer mass dismissals & replacements after interviews for permanent faculty, KC’s small team of 8 professors is involved not only with its heavily stacked schedule of Viksit Bharat events within the department (being the media representatives of the college) but also with the press & coverage of all others.

Continued on page 3 →

“Aane Do Dilli, Seedha Goli Maar Denge”- Middle-Class · continued from page 2

Parents of children in Board grades were concerned about traffic jams during their children’s papers. Borders blockages & disturbed traffic flow for people who commute in & out of the city have become matters of inconvenience, yet who they hold accountable is not the government who's taking these decisions but the protesters who are ‘compelling’ it to. There seems to be a collective amnesia over the fact that Delhi is not just the capital of the middle class in & around NCR but everyone, everywhere within the political boundary of this nation. That ‘Chalo Dilli’ has represented dissent, dignity, & being heard for none other than the common men who are silenced elsewhere in the country since before India was even a sovereign state.

What changed? What did the farmers do to them? What has made these normal, God-fearing men & women turn against their own kind so suddenly?

When did farmers become the enemy?

Unsubtle Influence: News & Mass Media

While it might be ideal for every citizen to know at least the basics, it is ultimately a fact that components & dynamics of the public sphere are not common knowledge. (Read Next Week: Critical Theory for the Layman: Why News Media Hides its Workings from the Common Man) This is no coincidence; the lack of transparency in the workings of mass communication models is in fact by design & the reason why they are so effective in directing public opinion. The next section will explain, without lingo or jargon, what precisely these workings are with regard to the farmers' protest.

‘Protesters or Rioters?’ The Problem with TV News

The march was again put on hold, awaiting another round of negotiations on Sunday. “When the meetings have started, if we move forward (towards Delhi) then how will meetings happen?" (Movement leader Jagjit Singh Dallewal, Charushree Chundawat, Zee Business). Update, 20th February 2024 : As of 20th February, another round of negotiations has failed , & the March resumes. Internet shutdowns in Punjab & Haryana have not been lifted, nor have border blockages.

Having established this timeline of events as it has taken place at several of Delhi’s borders, we must now look at the trajectory of its presentation & coverage in mainstream media & public perception.

Consider India Today’s broadcast of footage from the Shambhu border, titled “Protesters or Rioters?” referring to visible agitation there, after Haryana Police had fired teargas shells at unarmed civilian protesters.

A pointwise discussion of farmers pelting stones at the policemen standing atop vans & armory, and vandalizing safety barriers as a 'show of strength' was all the segment had to go on about as justification of the agenda, yet there were no questions raised about the policemen themselves 'inciting a riot' when the subject of them pelting stones back at farmers came up. A part of the crowd attempting to dismantle a safety barrier that showed it falling on top of them was discussed only as a humiliating failure of an out-of-control mob, rather than anything warranting sympathy or safety concern.

Largely, the defending counsel dismissed the petition as lacking ‘legal sanctity,’ & both parties have now been given time to exchange affidavits.

Discussion: How much power do the courts really have?

Just how regulated are the self-regulated?

Classes on Hold for ‘Viksit Bharat’; Principal Busy in · continued from page 2

With DU’s infamous academic calendar already lagging behind in the 2023-24 session as always (the even semester began a staggering 16 days after the commencement date marked on the university’s initial calendar, delaying examinations till the last week of May), ongoing faculty interviews, & the university being in the transition period of the NEP, students and faculty are already stretched thin in an attempt to complete syllabi, & these generic, unnecessary, school-like activities - being carried out under the guise of improving the reach of government schemes to secluded communities - are taking precious time away from near graduate students.

But instances like these aren’t limited to the University of Delhi. The participation statistics of the Viksit Bharat Mission quoted on their official website continue to grow, & the reality of this ‘participation’ as far as being conducted in higher education institutes is that is forced, involuntary, & consistently being carried out at the threat of academic sabotage. At the capital’s Netaji Subhash Technological University, students were handed out ‘Viksit Bharat’ promotional tasks as ‘assignments,’ failing to complete which would mean wasting their previous semester.

“We had to send in some idea related to viksit bharat. The college people wouldn’t return our previous semester marksheets otherwise.” says a third-year B.Tech student at NSUT’s east campus.

What business do the Universities partaking in these activities have to do so? What business does the government have making them?

What part of saturating government schemes is taking a selfie with a cardboard cutout of Narendra Modi & uploading it to a gov.in website?

Source: TVE

This is by & large the approach that TV news channels have adopted in discussing matters of police violence toward farmers at the borders. It seems as if the very act of protesting strips you of all dignity & humanity, & thus being treated inhumanely by the government is not only acceptable but understood. Their humiliation & injury are to be celebrated; their victories & competence are to be painted as acts of organised terror.

“Aane Do Dilli, Seedha Goli Maar Denge”- Middle-Class · continued from page 3

Billionaires, Congress Goons, & Khalistanis: Branding & Prejudice

We’ll club unintentionally satirical & cartoonish news channels (See: Capital TV: Chalo Delhi 2.0 LIVE: Farmers Protest 2024 Or A Khalistani Agenda, Know The Truth | Dr. Manish Kumar ) under the subhead of political commentators & miscellaneous opinion leaders in part two. For now, our assessment of public perception is concerned with the influence of formal & traditional news media, which follows at least structural if not ethical tenets of news production, & is taken seriously within the industry. An analysis of YouTube comments under India Today’s ‘Protesters or Rioters ’ broadcast revealed that large-scale support for farmers in the Indian diaspora has been replaced with the same prejudiced ideas that they had so harshly rejected the State for propagating 3 years ago, along with an added desire to see these men violently penalised, from the celebration of the militant attacks to demands for expulsion of these individuals to ‘Canada’ or ‘Pakistan.’ The hatred is communally charged & hungry to see the protesters hurt, with some even criticising the Modi regime for going too soft on them.

“Shameful comments in this forum. Calling farmers terrorists and more is a disgrace. Farmers all over north India in many states are protesting yet the media focus is on Punjab!! Punjabis are on the forefront just as Punjabis were on the forefront of fighting foreign invaders from Alexander to the Mughals. These people are not terrorists, far from!!” Supportive comments, though rare, can be found. But the unfortunate reality is that most of them come from the targeted community itself, defending, & not disagreeing.— Supportive comments, though rare, can be found. But the unfortunate reality is that most of them come from the targeted community itself, defending, & not disagreeing.

There are three primary assumptions that hostile audiences seem to be making about the protesters, with every farmer involved in the Chalo Dilli Andolan being one, some or all of the following, all contributing to a larger narrative that feels more ‘anti-Punjabi’ than anything else:

MEDIA

Editor’s Desk: Then They Came for the News

An editorial invoking Martin Niemöller's 'First They Came' as an allegory for the creeping suppression of the Indian press, and a statement on what The Voice Express is choosing to stand for in calling itself a publication, not just a student blog.

By Mouli Sharma

If you didn’t get that joke, then you perhaps haven’t heard of Martin Niemöller, a Nazi Sympathizer turned Holocaust victim, a particular speech of whose for many a German after the war transformed the image of the Nazi party from an overambitious & unfortunate political organization to the cartoonishly evil & genocidal monsters we know & love to condemn them as today. You see, good Christian Martin here wrote a poem (yes, a speech, really, but they called it a confessional poem, & for good reason so we’ll leave it at that), & it went something like this:

First they came for the socialists, and I did not speak out, Because I was not a socialist. Then they came for the trade unionists, and I did not speak out, Because I was not a trade unionist. Then they came for the Jews, and I did not speak out, Because I was not a Jew. Then they came for me, and there was no one left to speak for me. Martin Niemöller, 1946.— Martin Niemöller, 1946.

If you were here two months ago, you would remember a time when we hadn’t the confidence to call this little publication here even a news website, let alone a good, or – God forbid – honest one. Just college students trying to say what we think is worth saying, we called it instead. “Whatever literature you do find here, it isn’t yet news, not quite, but it does possess the beginnings of it,” we said.

“And it is in those beginnings that we hope to someday find the becoming’s of it, as well. Regardless of whether or not we’ll be any more qualified to declare them so then than we are now, & regardless of whether or not either of us has any business trying to find out. We might not, on both counts. But then again, what is youth if not fighting a war you did not start.”

As of 25th November 2023 (remember, remember), they’ve come first for the professors, & we’ve done nothing, because we are not professors. (Edit: As of March 2024, they've come for the activists, they've come for the farmers, they've come for the Muslims, they've come for the students, & they've come for the politicians, & we are much closer to an answer than we were five months ago, of exactly where in the line it is that our number falls.) So, it’s safe to say, that as of November 2023, our youth means nothing. And it’s about damn time then, that we start that war.

1. Khalistanis, i.e. separatist Sikh people who want a sovereign nation for the Punjabi-Sikh community within present Indian territory.
  2. Goons in bed with the opposition, the one in power in Punjab being the Indian National Congress.
  3. ‘Millionaire’ farmers, or less radically understood to be landowners as opposed to cultivators, unaffected by farm laws & agricultural policy.

As of yet, there is no linkage of any of the three farmers’ groups involved in the process with ‘Khalistan’ advocates, nor with terrorist groups. Their involvement with Congress is obvious speculation, which albeit natural, still lacks evidential basis. Given the intensive crackdown on the social media accounts & internet activities of those involved in or actively supporting the protest, large-scale or organised views of the country's agricultural masses have been shut down using British Era laws, which does no favours to the idea that the farmers complaints are anyhow disingenuous. On the contrary, nationwide participation in strikes like the Bharat Bandh which are a show of solidarity, suggests the opposite.

2021 vs 2024: Same Players, New Attitudes

It is important to note that, while hints & leads to these ideas may be found in the reportage of most news outlets, due to the striking groundlessness of each, none of the points listed out in the report itself validated any of these claims explicitly. Even government strategy has been a lot cleverer this time around, with spokesmen advertising diplomacy & violence hiding behind censorship & military policy. So what gives?

“No Khalistani elements. The Govt. failed to understand the demands of poor farmers.” “Poor farmers are beaten by police.”

In contrast, the majority of the (coherent) comments this time around are:

Continued on page 5 →

“Aane Do Dilli, Seedha Goli Maar Denge”- Middle-Class · continued from page 4
“These are not farmers, the nation knows their intentions. All these guys are millionaires.” “My prayers go out to these Policemen. Please be safe while braving these so-called farmers.” “corretion - KHALISTAN Protests 2.0” (sic) “Check these farmers' backgrounds. They could be Abduls and Ibrahims in the guise of Taqiya Singhs and Harami Singhs.” “These Punjab farmers are a nuisance. While other state farmers are busy working hard. These Punjab farmers are destroying public property.”

Communal prejudice & slurs litter these comment sections. Public theories are always more conspiracy than fact, hate speeches seldom contain citations, & at the end of the day, people do have a right to speculate. But hatred, like empathy, does not come from vacuum. Nothing does (read: Hitler's Propaganda Ministry: News is Not What You Think it Is). Even seemingly outlandish ideas are carefully engineered, whether intentionally or unintentionally. The opinions of those labeling all turban-wearing, tractor-driving farmers with communal slurs & vitriol are not entirely their own, just like those labeling them victims of a capitalist regime. You are a product of what you read, see & hear, & while there are aspects of choice to this exercise, the freedom is mostly illusory. Consider the following example:

Despite the brutality & lack of support they’ve been met with (except by opposition parties like Congress who have predictably taken a pro-kisaan anti-BJP stance), the farmers weather on. 2021’s ‘Chalo Dilli March’ was a victory, not only for farmers but for commoners of the entire nation, as the government finally repealed its 3 controversial farm laws after the year-long protest. But this victory did not come easy. A year-long protest on the roads of Delhi outskirts meant nights spent out in the December-January freezing temperatures & afternoons spent out during Loo season. By the end of the year, 248 farmers had lost their lives , including 8 who were killed.

Lessons from the 2021 protests have made the farmers better equipped for what is to come. They are prepared this time around, having brought trucks of food supplies & blankets that are nightly distributed among protest members; a community taking care of its own. The wounded & injured are tended to in these hours, patched up & rested for another day of fighting.

Now consider the fact that the same visuals of food & blanket distribution were broadcast on Indian News Channels with voiceovers of Khalistani & Anti-Punjabi rhetoric. The same clips doing the rounds on mainstream channels as well as more small TV networks broadcast these for entire lengths of programs, somehow managing to frame these men, many of them aged, all of them exhausted, as national security threats for eating food & taking care of each other.

These are not luxuries. Media perception & pseudointellectual attacks on the integrity of the movement seem to imply that a paper plate containing a handful of rice & spilling over dal is the height of decadence that these supposed ‘Kulaks,’ greedy, rich landlords hailing from Punjab are rewarding themselves with, blankets & tractors being evidence of their hoarded riches. Opinion articles in the present media sphere, written by civilians without necessary journalistic or academic qualifications, reflect this mentality.
